- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.7) and forecast is trending up, reduce forecast peak by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.  
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤0.3) and forecast is trending down, avoid excessive downward correction — allow slight mean reversion but don’t overcorrect.  
- If recent history shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of price decline), model should not overpredict further decline; adjust downward bias.  
- If forecast spikes sharply after a dip (e.g., 3–5 days of low prices), reduce forecast peak by 10–15% to account for lagged momentum.  
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating high/low), avoid overfitting to recent sentiment — use 3–5 day smoothing to filter noise.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome deviates >10% from forecast in first 5 days, adjust forecast downward for remaining days to reflect slower momentum.  
- If sentiment history shows consistent positive sentiment over 5+ days, forecast should not be below 10% below recent 5-day average.  
- If forecast is consistently above true outcome by >5% over 3–5 days, reduce forecast by 5–10% to reflect sentiment-driven overconfidence.
